1.title: Rules & your responsibilities
primer: Amateur Service = self-training, intercommunication, technical investigation. Never for gain or business.
ITU writes the International Radio Regulations; MBIE (Radio Spectrum Management) administers NZ. NZ is ITU Region 3.
Certificate (GAOC) + the GURL = your 'licence'. Certificate is for life, no minimum or maximum age. Keep it at the station.
You, the operator, are responsible for the signal. A qualified operator is needed whenever transmitting; unqualified family can't transmit alone.
Callsign: ZL + one digit 1–4 + letters (ZL2HF). Identify with your callsign, always. Relinquished callsigns rest 1 year.
Address change: tell RSM within 1 month. MBIE can inspect your certificate at any time and close you down.
Secret codes/ciphers: forbidden (except repeater/beacon control). Never knowingly interfere. Never disclose overheard traffic.
Third party: brief personal messages only, no fees. Distress: any means is allowed.
New operator: first 3 months only below 5 MHz and above 25 MHz; 50 contacts to unlock 5–25 MHz.
Power limit = whatever the GURL says for that band. Bandplans are NZART's: recommended, follow them. HF 3–30 MHz, VHF 30–300 MHz.

2.title: Bands & sharing
primer: Shared with other services: 40 m 7.1–7.3, 6 m 51–54, 2 m 146–148. 15 m 21–21.45 is primary (ours).
Secondary user = may use it, but must not cause harmful interference to the primary user.
Satellite bands: 28–29.7 MHz and 144–146 MHz (also 435–438).
130–190 kHz: 5 W eirp max. 60 m 15 W eirp. 32 cm 25 W.
Same frequency? Equal rights; the second-comer politely gives way.
'Frequency agile' = you can change frequency to avoid interfering.

3.title: Atoms, conductors, batteries
primer: Conductors: silver, copper, gold, aluminium. Insulators: plastic, ceramic, glass, porcelain, air.
Semiconductors: silicon, germanium. N-type carries electrons, P-type carries holes.
Metals: resistance rises with temperature.
Atom loses an electron → positive ion. Gains one → negative ion.
Current in a wire makes a magnetic field around it. Like poles repel.
Lead-acid, NiCd, Li-ion are rechargeable; alkaline AA is not.

4.title: Units & multipliers
primer: Volt V (pressure), Amp A (flow), Ohm Ω (resistance/impedance), Watt W, Farad F, Henry H.
Impedance = resistance combined with reactance.
Convert first: 250 mA = 0.25 A; 2 V = 2000 mV; 1 kΩ = 1000 Ω.

5.title: Ohm's Law
primer: E = I × R · I = E ÷ R · R = E ÷ I. Cover the one you want in the triangle.
Always turn mA into A (or kΩ into Ω) before calculating.
More voltage → more current (double V, double I).
mnemonics: Triangle: E on top, I and R below

6.title: Series & parallel resistors
primer: Series: add them. Total is bigger than the biggest. Same current everywhere; voltage splits.
Parallel: total is smaller than the smallest. Same voltage across each; currents add.
Equal resistors in parallel: R ÷ n. Two resistors: (A × B) ÷ (A + B).
Equal series lamps share the supply: six 2 V lamps need 12 V.
Voltage sag under load = battery internal resistance.

7.title: Power
primer: P = E × I. Also P = I²R and P = E²/R.
Double the voltage across a resistor → 4× the power.
A resistor burns because it dissipates too much power (not 'current' or 'voltage').
Series total power: find total R, then I, then P = E × I.
Heat = DC input power − RF output power.
mnemonics: Power triangle: P on top, E and I below

8.title: AC basics
primer: AC reverses direction periodically. Hz = cycles per second. NZ mains 230 V, 50 Hz.
RMS = 0.707 × peak. Peak = 1.414 × RMS. RMS is what meters and Ohm's law use.
A harmonic is a whole-number multiple (2 kHz → 4 kHz is the 2nd harmonic).
1 kHz = 1000 Hz · 1 MHz = 1000 kHz · 1 GHz = 1000 MHz.

9.title: Capacitors, inductors, resonance
primer: Capacitor: two plates + dielectric. Closer plates or bigger plates = more capacitance.
Capacitors in parallel add. In series: less than the smallest, but higher voltage rating.
Inductors in series add; in parallel they combine like resistors (two 20 µH → 10 µH). More turns = more inductance.
Capacitor passes AC, blocks DC. Xc falls as frequency rises.
Inductor passes DC, blocks high-frequency AC. XL = 2πfL rises as frequency rises.
Resonance: XL = XC. Series LC: impedance minimum. Parallel LC: impedance maximum.
High Q = very selective (narrow). Transformer: voltage follows the turns ratio (100:10 → 230 V becomes 23 V).
mnemonics: Series = Smallest impedance, Parallel = Peak impedance

10.title: Safety
primer: Own safety first: switch off the power BEFORE touching a shocked person or opening gear. Then unplug.
RCD trips when phase and neutral currents are not equal.
Earth wire stops the chassis becoming live in a fault (fuse blows).
Colours: brown = live (phase), blue = neutral, green/yellow = earth.
Isolating transformer: no voltage between either output lead and earth.
mnemonics: Brown = live, Blue = neutral, Green/yellow = earth

11.title: Semiconductors
primer: Diode: one way, anode → cathode. Silicon drops ~0.7 V, germanium ~0.3 V. Power supplies use silicon.
Diodes also demodulate (detect) radio signals.
Zener = voltage regulator. Varactor = variable capacitor.
Bipolar transistor: NPN or PNP, three leads: base, collector, emitter. It amplifies.
FET: gate, drain, source; N-channel or P-channel.
Doping = adding impurities. Transistors die from heat. Cut-off = base at emitter potential.
mnemonics: Zener = voltage regulator; varactor = variable capacitor

12.title: Symbols
primer: Bipolar: NPN arrow points out, PNP arrow points in.
JFET: N-channel arrow points in, P-channel out.
Dual-gate MOSFET has 2 gates + source + drain.
Valve: P plate, S screen grid, G control grid, C cathode, H heater.

13.title: Meters
primer: Ammeter: in SERIES, very low resistance. Across a car battery = short circuit.
Voltmeter: in PARALLEL, very high resistance.
Ohmmeter measures resistance between its terminals. SWR meter 'reverse' = reflected power.
RMS meter on a sine wave reads 0.707 × peak (14 V peak → ~10 V).
mnemonics: Amps in a Series line, Volts in Parallel

14.title: Decibels
primer: In cascade, dB simply add. Attenuators subtract.
dBi vs isotropic · dBd vs dipole · dBm vs 1 mW · dBW vs 1 W.
EIRP limit: transmitter dBW + antenna gain − feedline loss.

15.title: HF station layout
primer: Chain: transceiver → (linear amp) → low-pass filter → SWR bridge → antenna switch/tuner → antenna or dummy load.
Low-pass filter stops anything above 30 MHz reaching the antenna.
Dummy load: 50 Ω, doesn't radiate, has a power rating. SWR bridge compares forward and reflected power.
Linear amp output is a bigger copy of the input. Tuner = matcher.
mnemonics: Filter first, then watch (SWR), then switch

16.title: Receiver block diagrams
primer: Superhet: antenna → RF amp → mixer (+ oscillator) → filter → IF amp → product detector (+ BFO) → AF amp → speaker. Signal flows left to right.
RF amp: boosts the signal ahead of the noisy mixer and must be low-noise. Mixer: combines the signal and oscillator to make the intermediate frequency (IF); its input is tuned, its output is fixed.
The oscillator frequency differs from both the signal and the IF. The filter removes unwanted mixer outputs and sets the passband: CW ~500 Hz, SSB ~3 kHz, AM ~6 kHz, FM ~10 kHz.
Most of the gain is in the IF amp. Product detector + BFO bring SSB/CW down to audio. AF amp lifts the audio (speech frequencies) to drive the speaker; the volume control belongs to it.
FM receiver: IF is wider; a limiter removes amplitude variations/noise; the demodulator (discriminator or phase-locked loop) recovers the audio.

SDR: low/band-pass filter → RF low-noise amp → A-to-D → DSP (digital signal processing: demodulates, and is where software is loaded) → D-to-A → audio amp. Sample rate must be at least twice the top frequency (150 MHz → 6 m).
mnemonics: Left to right: antenna, RF, mixer, filter, IF, detector, audio

17.title: Receiver operation
primer: Stability = stays tuned (depends on the local oscillator). Sensitivity = hears weak signals (low internal noise, judged by signal+noise to noise ratio). Selectivity = separates close signals (narrow IF filter = high selectivity).
Tuning changes the local oscillator (and the RF/mixer input), not the IF. The BFO runs near the IF frequency and beats with it for a tone (CW) or replaces the missing carrier (SSB).
Mixer outputs sum AND difference: 7 + 16 = 23 and 16 − 7 = 9 MHz.

Image frequency is 2 × IF away from the wanted signal, on the same side as the oscillator (21 MHz with 500 kHz IF and oscillator above → image at 22 MHz). Higher IF or double conversion improves image rejection.
Oscillators counted with the BFO/CIO: single-conversion SSB has 2; double-conversion has two IFs and two local oscillators (plus the BFO).
Squelch silences noise when no signal. AGC = automatic gain control. RF amp raises sensitivity. Audio transformer matches the amp to the ~8 Ω speaker. SDR: I and Q signals 90° apart.

18.title: Transmitter block diagrams
primer: CW: oscillator (runs continuously, crystal for stability) → driver/buffer (isolates the oscillator from keying, stops chirp) → power amplifier; the Morse key lets the signal pass only when pressed. Signal = RF keyed on and off.
AM: carrier + two sidebands. Balanced modulator: no carrier, two sidebands. Filter then removes one sideband → SSB.

SSB: oscillator + speech amp → balanced modulator → filter → mixer (with VFO) translates the signal to the output frequency → linear amplifier (keeps the waveform, only raises amplitude). VFO = variable frequency oscillator.

FM: speech amp → modulator (audio shifts the oscillator frequency) → oscillator → frequency multiplier (makes a harmonic, brings it up to the RF) → power amp. Signal's frequency varies with the modulating waveform.
Linear amplification is needed for SSB/AM; FM can use non-linear amplifiers. Power amp raises the RF signal to a suitable level.

19.title: Transmitter theory
primer: Modulation puts information onto a carrier. SSB occupies about half the bandwidth of AM; Morse is an interrupted carrier.
SSB linear amp is rated in PEP: the average power at the crest of the modulating envelope. Linear = output is a bigger copy of the input.
Driver is before the final power amp; the final amp raises the power to the antenna. Output power is less than DC input; the difference is dissipated as heat.
FM distorted? Deviation too high. Stable VFO: regulated DC supply.

20.title: Harmonics & parasitics
primer: Harmonics are multiples of the fundamental from non-linear action or a distorted sine wave (3525 kHz → 7050 kHz is the 2nd; 7 MHz → 21 MHz 3rd, 35 MHz 5th; 28 MHz → 56 MHz 2nd).

Causes: overdriven/overloaded stages, over-modulation (flat-topping; turn the mic gain down). Fixes: tuned-circuit coupling between stages, wave trap for one harmonic, low-pass filter at the transmitter output.
Harmonics made in a receiver cause cross-modulation or intermodulation. Rusty metal joints (gutters, roofs) can act as diodes and make harmonics.

Parasitics: unwanted oscillations in high-gain stages with no mathematical link to the operating frequency (high or low). Cure: VHF chokes, ferrite beads or small 'stopper' resistors near the active device.
Spurious = unwanted emission unrelated to the output frequency.

21.title: Power supplies
primer: Chain: fuse in the mains (phase/active) lead → transformer → rectifier → filter (smoothing capacitor) → DC.
Transformer: output voltage follows the turns ratio (230 V, secondary half the turns → 115 V). Power out can't exceed power in.
Half-wave rectifier: one diode, ripple 50 Hz. Full-wave (centre-tap) and bridge (four diodes, no centre-tap): ripple 100 Hz (NZ mains).
Electrolytic smoothing capacitors: large value, small and cheap, polarity matters. 12 V 1 A supply → about 10,000 µF.
All supplies have internal resistance → voltage sags as current is drawn. A regulator cuts this. A 12 V car battery can run a 25 W VHF rig; a 500 mA plug-pack or AA cells can't.

22.title: Regulated supplies
primer: Regulated supply: transformer (AC to a convenient AC voltage) → rectifier (AC to pulsing DC) → filter (smooths) → regulator (holds the output constant).
Regulator can be a zener (small loads), a three-terminal chip, or a series-pass transistor (for higher current than a zener/three-terminal regulator can supply).
Diode reverse across a regulator: bypasses it if the output goes higher than the input. A diode in the input line guards against reversed polarity.
Crowbar across the output: last-ditch protection if the regulator fails. Fires a shorting device, blows the mains fuse.
Current limiting: keeps short-circuit current through the regulator/pass transistor small.

23.title: Operating procedure
primer: CQ = 'seek you'. LISTEN first, then ask if the frequency is in use. Keep calls short, use your callsign often.
Voice CQ: 'CQ CQ CQ this is ZL3QL ZL3QL ZL3QL'. In a callsign exchange, their callsign first, then yours.
Phonetics: Zulu Lima One Alpha November; Victor Kilo Five Zulu X-ray.
Signal report '5 and 1' = perfectly readable, very weak. 'Up 2' = listening 2 kHz higher.
Don't tune up at full power or on a repeater's input. Don't use excess audio drive (splatter).
Repeaters: pause about 3 seconds between overs, keep overs short (about 3 minutes max). 'Fully quieting' = your signal is strong enough to be noise-free. Announce 'ZL2ZZZ listening on 6675'.

24.title: Practical operating
primer: Repeater: receiver + transmitter + duplexer, carrier-operated. Weak mobile signal → repeater 'drops out'. 2 m split: +600 kHz above 147 MHz, −600 kHz on or below. 70 cm: ±5 MHz. National System = linked 70 cm repeaters.

Receiver controls: RF gain (ahead of the mixer, helps front-end overload), AF gain, AGC (keeps level steady as signals fade), squelch (mutes with no signal), noise blanker (mutes impulse noise such as ignition), S-meter (relative signal strength only).

Transceiver: PTT push-to-talk; VOX voice-operated transmit (fast attack, slow release); break-in keying lets you hear between Morse elements; RIT tunes only the receiver a few kHz; split = TX and RX on different frequencies.
ALC prevents over-driving the linear amp. Tune an ATU for minimum reflected power on the SWR bridge. Pileup = many stations calling one rare DX station.

25.title: Q signals
primer: QRM = Man-made interference ('your transmission is being interfered with'). QRN = Natural noise ('I am troubled by static').
QRL? = are you busy? (is the frequency in use?). QRZ? = who is calling me? QTH? = what is your location?
QRS = send slower. QRQ = send quicker. QRP? = shall I decrease power (QRP = low power). QSB = your signals are fading. QSY? = shall I change to another frequency?
mnemonics: QRM = Man-made, QRN = Natural; QRS = Slower, QRQ = Quicker

26.title: Transmission lines
primer: Two types: balanced parallel/open-wire (ribbon, ladder; 300–600 Ω) and unbalanced coax (inner conductor + insulation + braid). Most amateurs use 50 Ω coax; TV coax is 75 Ω.
Characteristic impedance depends on conductor size and spacing, not length. A line terminated in its characteristic impedance looks infinitely long (a cut-off piece keeps the same impedance).
Mismatch → reflected power, standing waves, heat in the PA, less radiated power. Losses rise with SWR, frequency and length. Transceivers cut power above ~2:1 SWR. SWR meter measures it.
Antenna tuner just transforms the impedance seen by the transmitter. Quarter-wave line inverts the load: shorted → very high (infinite), open → very low. Half-wave line repeats the load.
Open-wire: lowest loss but keep away from metal, can't be buried. Coax can be buried and run near metal. Velocity factor: solid polythene coax 0.66, twin line 0.82.
Balun joins balanced to unbalanced; unun joins unbalanced to unbalanced of a different impedance. Switch for one antenna on TX and RX should disable the unit not in use.

27.title: Antennas
primer: λ (m) = 300 ÷ MHz. Half-wave ≈ 150 ÷ MHz (the wire is ~2% shorter in practice; the exam rounds, so pick the closest). 25 MHz → 12 m; 1 MHz → 150 m; 7.1 MHz → about 20 m.
Dipole = half-wave, fed in the centre (max current, low voltage); ends are high voltage, low current. Free-space impedance ~73 Ω; folded dipole 4× = 300 Ω. Length mainly sets the resonant frequency.
Longer = lower frequency; shorter = higher. Series inductance or loading coils lower the frequency (shorter antenna, same electrical length). Insulators limit the electrical length.
A dipole cut for 40 m (7 MHz) also works on 15 m (three half-waves). Parallel-tuned traps in each leg give multi-band operation.
Quarter-wave ground plane: vertical, all directions, 50 Ω coax matches, good for a car roof at 28 MHz. 5/8 wave on VHF: low take-off angle. Verticals suit DX (low angle).

Yagi: driven element + parasitic reflector (behind, slightly longer) and directors (in front, slightly shorter), on a boom. Maximum radiation toward the director end. Gain comes from concentrating radiation in one direction.

Dipole is 2.15 dB above isotropic (hypothetical point source). Polarisation = direction of the E field; E and H fields are perpendicular. Bandwidth = range of frequencies the antenna works over (high gain → narrower).
Balun: balanced to unbalanced. Dummy antenna: 50 Ω non-inductive resistor, doesn't radiate; watch its power/time rating.
mnemonics: Wavelength = 300 ÷ MHz; half-wave is half that

28.title: Propagation
primer: Layers: D (day only, absorbs everything below ~4 MHz), E (~110 km, reflects high-angle low-band signals; fades at night), F (splits F1/F2 by day, merges at night; carries DX).

Ionisation peaks around noon in summer, lowest just before dawn. Sunspot cycle ≈ 11 years; solar flares → fade-outs. MUF = highest frequency reflected; above it, signals go into space. 28 MHz is best in daylight.

Ground wave: follows the earth, shorter range at higher frequency. Sky wave (ionospheric): bounces back, carries HF DX beyond 4000 km. Skip zone = between the end of the ground wave and where the sky wave lands; skip distance = to the nearest sky-wave landing.
Low take-off angle (< 30°) → longer hops and skip distance. Higher layer → longer skip.
Fading = changing path lengths (multipath); selective fading distorts AM. Sporadic-E: summer patches in the E layer.
VHF/UHF: line of sight, reflect off buildings, pass through the ionosphere to satellites. Polarisation matters on VHF, not on HF. Radio waves travel at the speed of light.
mnemonics: D absorbs, E sporadic, F for DX

29.title: Interference & filtering
primer: EMC = equipment works in its environment without causing or suffering intolerable interference.

Harmonics → narrow-band interference. Motor commutation, power lines (worse when wet) → broadband noise. Hum on your signal → regulated DC supply. Wide signal → over-driven audio stages. Key clicks → shape the keying (key-click filter).
Cross-modulation = strong signal rectified in the victim's receiver; you hear it behind the wanted signal. If it overloads the audio stages it is heard wherever the receiver is tuned.

Low-pass: passes below the cut-off, blocks above. High-pass: the opposite. Band-pass: attenuates each side of a band. Band-stop/notch: passes each side, removes a narrow band. Fit the low-pass filter at the transmitter output (attenuates above 30 MHz).
Toroid/choke on the feedline cuts common-mode interference. Op-amp: very high gain (reduced by feedback), very high input impedance, negative feedback in active filters.
Neighbour complains? Check your log, make sure your own domestic gear is fine, use minimum power. Field strength unit: volts per metre.
mnemonics: Low-pass at the TX output kills harmonics

30.title: Digital modes
primer: Modem = modulator/demodulator; a computer sound card can do it. Digital modes: FT8, RTTY, PSK31. FSK = frequency shift keying.
FT8 uses forward error correction. APRS = Automatic Packet Reporting System, FM on VHF/UHF.
Multipath errors on HF: lower the baud rate. Binary: 219 = 11011011 (128+64+16+8+2+1).
Encryption/secret codes are not allowed on amateur radio.
